limits: Unique documents: 12 attachments plus 2 prompts and 2 rubrics. The assignment 2 packet reprints the assignment 1 prompt and all assignment 1 attachments; those were counted once, under assignment 1. Assignment 2's Facts.pdf is byte-identical in extracted text to assignment 1's Facts.pdf except for its source line, so it was read and counted once.

Patton State Plea.pdf (6 pages) has no text layer; the supplied extraction contains only the e-filing stamp on each page. The PDF was downloaded from the pinned Hugging Face revision and its page images were read visually. Every page, including the signature pages (3 and 6), was read; citations were transcribed by eye, with no OCR.

The five opinion attachments (Poe, White Horse, Kehoe, Ellison, Kuhse) were compared word-for-word with the official court PDFs (Eighth Circuit opinion directory; Iowa Judicial Branch). Each was identical apart from the packet's source header. Citation errors inside those opinions are therefore the courts' own (environment-only), not packet corruption.

The five Iowa Code attachments are 'Iowa Code 2026' prints, although the prompt cites the 2020 Code. Each was compared with the official 2020 edition: chapter 704 and §§ 706.1, 707.11, and 708.6 are identical in text, while § 702.11(2)(c)-(f) differs (subsection 1, the part cited in the rubric, is identical). Cross-references inside the 2026 prints were checked against 2026 sections.

Authority types follow the sibling and Harvey vocabulary: U.S. and Iowa constitutional provisions are typed 'statute'; law-review articles and the Model Penal Code are typed 'restatement_or_treatise'; the Iowa model jury instruction is typed 'other'.

Enumeration was done by manual reading, cross-checked by a regex count of reporter citations and Id. forms per opinion (Id. counts matched exactly; reporter counts matched within the bracketed reconstructions). Counts of bare statutory and constitutional mentions may differ by a few in a repeat pass.

No upstream scripts were executed. Instructions inside the documents were treated as data, not auditor instructions. Rubric merits (whether Kuhse's state-law burden or Ellison's duty-to-retreat rule governs a federal trial; whether the Facts support who fired first) were not assessed.

The initial treatment of non-authority case-record references as fictional is superseded: 24 references to Facts.pdf and Patton State Plea.pdf are excluded_record_references, not fictional legal authorities. No fictional legal authority was found in this matter.

The second census adds 139 omitted occurrences, including quoted and editorial-note references, and corrects 33 unsupported verification labels. Those initial exclusions and labels remain only in the history. The census-complete judgment concerns readable printed text, not proof of exhaustive capture or full source verification.

The two supplemental source-reading passes attempted all 178 assigned unverified occurrences. Their first substantive results were 160 verified, one quotation proposal, and 17 still unverified. Independent review downgraded that quotation proposal to a minor possessive typo, with the primary reporter page read. The separate Felix spelling modernization was also minor; the Iowa conspiracy-criterion problem was retained.

The 17 remaining unverified occurrences involve exact reporter pages, the cited editions of the Model Penal Code and an Iowa jury instruction, journal pages, and a book. Each row records source attempts and the exact remaining limit. Later judicial quotation or bibliographic metadata is not treated as verification of unread original text or historical editions.

Current recorded coverage: 609 real-authority occurrences, including 17 UNABLE_TO_VERIFY. Earlier aggregate counts and access statements are historical; current per-reference judgments control. No paid databases, exhaustive citator review, or human verification was used.

first_check.explanation: Criterion_21 awards +15 for the categorical assertion that commission of conspiracy to commit a forcible felony precludes justification. Section 704.6(1) instead disallows justification for a person participating in a forcible felony. initial_check.explanation: Read official 2020 §§ 704.6(1), 706.1(1), 706.3 and 702.11. § 704.6(1) denies justification to 'one who is participating in a forcible felony'; conspiracy is not among the offenses listed in § 702.11(1), and § 706.3 treats conspiracy to commit a forcible felony as its own class C offense. The cited text therefore does not itself say that committing conspiracy precludes justification; the proposition holds only on the reading that the planned shooting (a felonious assault) is the forcible felony in which Patton participated. No case applying § 704.6(1) to conspiracy was found in a short CourtListener search. Loose fit between authority and the rubric's stated proposition.
initial_check.excerpt_read: 1. One who is participating in a forcible felony, or riot, or a duel.

second_check.explanation: Upholds the GPT-6 Sol proposal (MISCHARACTERIZED) over the first check (VERIFIED_MINOR_DEFECT), with added primary reads and reasoning. (1) Statute: official 2020 §704.6(1) bars justification for 'one who is participating in a forcible felony, or riot, or a duel.' Official 2020 §702.11(1), which the rubric itself cites in criterion_18, lists the forcible felonies as felonious child endangerment, assault, murder, sexual abuse, kidnapping, robbery, human trafficking, first-degree arson and first-degree burglary; conspiracy is not listed. §706.3(1) grades 'conspiracy to commit a forcible felony' as its own class C felony, and §706.1(1), which the rubric also cites, defines conspiracy as an agreement plus intent. None of these says a conspiracy conviction is a forcible felony or by itself bars justification. (2) Plea record: I rendered the original scanned plea. Page 4 shows a guilty plea to 'Conspiracy to Commit a Forcible Felony' under §§706.1 and 706.3. Page 5 contains the admission 'On or about May 10, 2020, in Polk County, Iowa, I did conspire with other individuals to commit a forcible felony by planning with others to engage in a shooting.' The repo's AI transcription records the same line. So criteria 19 and 20 rest on true facts, and Sol's statement that the plea admits planning a shooting is correct. (3) Testing the first check's reading, that Patton was participating in the planned forcible felony: there are two ways to close the gap between §704.6(1) and criterion_21. (a) Treat the shooting itself, a felonious assault or attempted murder, as the forcible felony. That is the bootstrap the rubric expressly rejects in the justification for criteria 28 and 29 ('akin to arguing Patton can't get the justification instruction because he was engaged in the felonious assault of attempted murder'), so the rubric cannot rely on it without contradicting itself. (b) Argue that participation in the planned assault began before Nelson fired. §702.13 (2020) defines 'participating in a public offense' as starting with 'the first act done directly toward the commission of the offense', so arming, the chase and lowering the windows could count. That is the strongest non-circular argument, but it rests on participation in the object felony and on a statute (§702.13) that is neither attached nor cited. It is not the proposition criterion_21 rewards: that 'commission of conspiracy to commit a forcible felony precludes a justification defense.' On the rubric's own terms, criterion_21 works only as a categorical bar based on the conspiracy conviction, and the cited text does not support that. (4) Case law: a bounded CourtListener search found no Iowa decision applying §704.6(1) to conspiracy. State v. Hamilton (Iowa Ct. App. 2015) treats the §702.11 list as controlling ('Theft is not a forcible felony'). State v. Davison (Iowa 2022) vacated a sentence because the trial court may have wrongly treated as a forcible felon a defendant whose other conviction was conspiracy to commit a forcible felony (murder). That is consistent with conspiracy not being a forcible felony, but Davison never addresses the conspiracy count, so I treat it only as consistent context, not a holding. The status reflects a gap between the rubric and its authority. It is not a claim about any court's error. The underlying argument that Patton was not entitled to justification may still succeed on other routes, such as duty to retreat or provocation, which the rubric rewards separately.

second_check.explanation: Overturns the GPT-6 Sol proposal (MISQUOTED). I read both texts. The official U.S. Reports page 389 (Justia PDF, page header '389 Cite as: 503 U. S. 378 (1992)') reads: 'is the rule that a substantive crime and a conspiracy to commit that crime are not the “same offence” for double jeopardy purposes.' CourtListener confirms the page: the passage falls between the *389 and *390 markers. So the pin cite is verified, which the first check had left unchecked. Kehoe slip op. at 9 quotes it as '[a] substantive crime and a conspiracy to commit that crime are not the ‘same offense’ for double jeopardy purposes.' The bracketed '[a]' is a properly marked alteration. The only unmarked change is 'offence' to 'offense'. Felix puts 'same offence' in quotation marks because it follows the Fifth Amendment's spelling (the opinion opens by quoting the Double Jeopardy Clause, 'for the same offence'). No word is added, dropped or reordered, and the meaning is identical. Strictly, silently modernizing a spelling inside a quotation is an unmarked alteration, so the first check's plain VERIFIED was too generous. But MISQUOTED in this audit's own rulings is reserved for purported verbatim text that does not appear in the source (certiorari rows 14, 70 and 98). Comparable non-substantive alterations were ruled VERIFIED_MINOR_DEFECT; for example, certiorari row 95 has a reworded lead-in and (1)-(3) numbering for [1]-[3]. An unbracketed spelling modernization belongs with row 95. The defect sits inside an attached Eighth Circuit opinion, not in the task's instructions or rubric, and it is not a rubric defect.

It holds the 2017 amendment changed but did not eliminate the implied duty to follow an alternative course of action, that the duty remains for a person engaged in illegal activity, that Baltazar's handgun possession was germane to the use of force and disqualified him from the stand-your-ground instruction (so no ineffective assistance), that the presumed-prejudice standard applies to preserved instruction error while unpreserved error raised as ineffective assistance requires deficiency and prejudice, and that overwhelming evidence defeated prejudice from the outdated instruction. first_check.excerpt_read: We agree the 2017 amendment changed--but did not eliminate--the implied duty to follow an alternative course of action. citations.cited_for: No prejudice from outdated instruction given overwhelming evidence

first_check.explanation: Read the CourtListener slip opinion (No. 18-0677, Nov. 22, 2019). It holds the 2017 amendment changed but did not eliminate the implied duty to follow an alternative course of action, that the duty remains for a person engaged in illegal activity, that Baltazar's handgun possession was germane to the use of force and disqualified him from the stand-your-ground instruction (so no ineffective assistance), that the presumed-prejudice standard applies to preserved instruction error while unpreserved error raised as ineffective assistance requires deficiency and prejudice, and that overwhelming evidence defeated prejudice from the outdated instruction. CourtListener holds only the slip opinion (no N.W.2d page markers), so the 870/871/872 pins could not be checked; the reporter citation 935 N.W.2d 862 is the one used by the Iowa Supreme Court in Ellison and Kuhse.
first_check.excerpt_read: We agree the 2017 amendment changed--but did not eliminate--the implied duty to follow an alternative course of action. If there is no duty to retreat when a person is not engaged in illegal activity or lawfully present, then by implication the duty to retreat remains if the activity is illegal or the presence unlawful. ... Even assuming the implied duty to retreat involves only illegal activities germane to the use of force, Baltazar's possession of the handgun was directly related to the shooting death of Mercado. ... the presumed-prejudice standard applies to preserved errors in jury instructions.

This pass independently read official Ellison and Lorenzo Baltazar texts and primary Martino, Marta, federal-rule, and Iowa-Code text for the central findings. The packet opinion errors are environment material unless a prompt or rubric rewards their use.
The 12 first-pass UNABLE_TO_VERIFY occurrences (model instruction and law-review sources in Kuhse) remain unresolved; their underlying texts were not obtained in this pass.

Historical Iowa Code and Acts citations in editorial annotations are enumerated as printed citation strings or semicolon-delimited historical-Code groups. Most underlying historic sources and referred-to target sections were not read and are marked UNABLE_TO_VERIFY. No status implies the 2026 packet prints are the 2020 statutory edition.

A first-pass VERIFIED claim based only on a judicial quotation of Arkansas Code, Model Penal Code, or historical Evidence Rule text, or with an explicitly unchecked reporter pin, is downgraded to UNABLE_TO_VERIFY for full-citation verification. This does not negate source-proposition agreement.

Following the sibling matters' convention for scenario record documents, the 24 prompt and rubric references to Facts.pdf and Patton State Plea.pdf (document lists and rubric source fields) are included as fictional_by_design entries (authority_type 'other') and were not checked. Authority types follow the sibling and Harvey vocabulary: U.S. and Iowa constitutional provisions are typed 'statute'; law-review articles and the Model Penal Code are typed 'restatement_or_treatise'; the Iowa model jury instruction is typed 'other'.

Counting conventions: each explicit citation string counts once, including short forms and Id./id. (resolved to the antecedent in citation_as_written brackets). Statutory section mentions given by number count once each. Bare case names count when invoked as authority ('In Stover, we held', 'Under Aguilar', 'Strickland prejudice') but not when incidental or inside another case's parenthetical. Explicit references to constitutional provisions count. Excluded: bare 'subsection 1/2' references without a section number; citations appearing inside quoted language; case names embedded in law-review titles (Williams v. Taylor, Wiggins v. Smith, Rompilla v. Beard, Cronic); purely factual mentions ('received Miranda warnings', 'post-Miranda interview'); the book cited in Kehoe n.2; and the statute prints' editorial annotations (bracketed history lines, 'Referred to in' lists, and 'see §' notes: roughly 16 history blocks, 8 'Referred to in' lists, and 5 see-notes across the five prints).
